title: Isomorphism of tree-automatic ordinals without addition
formal: Is there an algorithm which, given two injective finite-tree-automatic presentations promised to describe well-orders using only their domain and strict order relations, decides whether those well-orders are isomorphic?
definitions:
A code is a finite rooted ordered binary tree with labels in a finite alphabet. Every node has either zero or two children. A finite bottom-up tree automaton assigns a state to a leaf from its label, and to an internal node from its label and its children’s states; acceptance means the root receives a designated accepting state in some run. A presentation consists of an automaton for a language D of codes and an automaton for the relation < on D. To recognize a pair, read their convolution: use the union of their tree domains and pad a missing component by a new blank symbol.

Codes are the elements themselves, so distinct accepted trees represent distinct elements; no quotient or equality automaton is supplied. The promise is that < is a strict linear order on D and every nonempty subset of D has a least element. Empty D is allowed and denotes ordinal zero. The promise is semantic, not a finite proof or ordinal notation attached to the input. Isomorphism means existence of a bijection between the domains preserving and reflecting <. Only domain and order automata are supplied: there is no presentation of ordinal addition.

A decision procedure must halt and be correct on every pair satisfying the promise. It may behave arbitrarily on inputs violating it. No complexity bound is requested, and the task does not include deciding whether an arbitrary presentation is well-founded.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked promise-decision algorithm with termination and correctness on all well-order presentations, or a complete undecidability proof whose reduction always produces valid well-order presentations. A procedure requiring an additional automaton for ordinal addition does not meet the input specification.
context:
Jain, Khoussainov, Schlicht and Stephan decide isomorphism when the presentations also supply ordinal addition. Their introduction distinguishes the order-only problem.

Knowing that an ordinal has some presentation with addition does not construct that extra relation on an arbitrary given order presentation. This is the input distinction retained here.
why: The problem tests whether ordinal structure can be compared algorithmically without an additional automatic addition operation.
